p3-1-2.text: The toy boat floats on water. Does it need water to live?
options: No. It floats on water but does not use it.
Yes. It floats on the pond all day, so it must need water.
Yes. It gets wet, so it must need water.
p3-1-2.why: Floating on water is not the same as needing it. The boat is non-living. It does not need water, food or air.

p3-1-2.text: What does the bean plant need to stay alive and grow?
p3-1-2.why: The bean plant is living. It needs water, food and air to stay alive and grow.

p3-1-2.text: A toy boat moves across a pond when the wind blows. Is it living?
options: No. The wind pushes it. It does not need food.
Yes. It moves across the pond, so it is living.
Yes. It is on the water, so it is living.
p3-1-2.why: Moving in the wind is not a clue for living. A living thing needs water, food and air, and can grow.

p3-1-2.text: Why does a bean plant need air?
options: Living things need air to stay alive.
Air makes the plant float on water.
Air keeps its leaves dry in the rain.
p3-1-2.why: All living things need air. The bean plant used the air it was given.

p3-1-2.text: Which of these needs water, food and air?
p3-1-2.why: A kitten is living, so it needs water, food and air. The boat, the stone and the kite are non-living.

p3-1-3.text: A toy chick moves when it is wound up. Is it living?
options: No. It moves, but it does not need food or air.
Yes. It moves when it is wound up, so it is living.
Yes. It looks like a baby chick, so it is living.
Yes. It makes a sound, so it is living.
p3-1-3.why: One clue is not enough. A living thing shows all six clues. A wound-up toy shows only movement.

p3-1-3.text: How many of the six clues does a living thing show?
p3-1-3.why: The hen showed all six clues. The lamp showed none. Living things show all six.

p3-1-3.text: A kite flies high in the wind. Is it living?
options: No. The wind moves it. It does not need food.
Yes. It flies high in the sky, so it is living.
Yes. It is up in the air, so it must need air.
Yes. It is colourful, so it is living.
p3-1-3.why: A kite only moves because the wind pushes it. It shows none of the six clues.

p3-1-3.text: Which clue shows that a goldfish is living?
options: It is orange with shiny scales.
It lives in a bowl on a shelf.
It is small and fits in a hand.
p3-1-3.why: Eating, growing, needing water and air, responding and making young ones are the clues. Colour and size are not.

p3-1-3.text: What does "respond" mean for a living thing?
options: It reacts to a change around it.
It gives out light in a dark room.
It floats on a pond in the sun.
It is heavy and hard to lift.
p3-1-3.why: Living things respond to changes around them. The hen moved when something changed. The lamp did not.

p3-2-1a.text: A hibiscus has no flower open today. Which group is it in?
options: Flowering. It can make a flower.
Non-flowering, because no flower is open now.
p3-2-1a.why: A flowering plant does not always have a flower open. It still belongs to the flowering group.

p3-2-1a.text: A tall plant can never make a flower. Which group is it in?
options: Flowering, because it has leaves and roots.
p3-2-1a.why: Only one thing decides the group: can it make a flower? Height, leaves and roots do not.

p3-2-1a.text: A short spiky plant has spore bags under its leaves. Which group is it in?
options: Flowering, because it is short and small.
p3-2-1a.why: Spore bags are the clue. Plants with spores do not make flowers. Being spiky is not the rule.

p3-2-1a.text: What do flowering plants use to make seeds?
p3-2-1a.why: Flowering plants make seeds inside a flower.

p3-2-1a.text: What do non-flowering plants like ferns use to reproduce?
p3-2-1a.why: Non-flowering plants make spores instead of flowers.

p3-2-1b.text: An animal with eight legs sits on a web. Is it an insect?
options: No. An insect has six legs. This is a spider.
Yes. It is small and has a hard body, so it is an insect.
Yes. It has no fur, so it is an insect.
Yes. It sits on a web in the garden, so it is an insect.
p3-2-1b.why: Count the legs. An insect has six legs and a hard case. Eight legs is a spider.

p3-2-1b.text: A furry animal swims and feeds its young with milk. What is it?
options: A mammal, because it has fur and milk.
A fish, because it swims and lives in water.
A fish, because it swims and has no legs.
An amphibian, because it swims in ponds.
p3-2-1b.why: Living in water does not always mean fish. Fur and feeding young with milk are mammal clues.

p3-2-1b.text: A feathered animal cannot fly. Is it a bird?
options: No. It cannot fly high in the sky, so it is not a bird.
No. It walks on land on two legs, so it is a reptile.
No. Only flying animals are birds.
p3-2-1b.why: Feathers, not flight, decide the group. A bird that cannot fly is still a bird.

p3-2-1b.text: An animal has moist skin and lays its eggs in water. What is it?
options: A fish, because it lives in water.
A reptile, because it has four legs.
A mammal, because it has skin.
p3-2-1b.why: Moist skin and eggs laid in water are the amphibian clues, like the frog.

p3-2-1b.text: How many legs does an insect have?
options: Any number, if it is small.
p3-2-1b.why: An insect has six legs and a hard case. Eight legs is a spider.

p3-2-2.text: Why do we need a microscope to see bacteria?
options: They are too tiny to see with our eyes.
They move too fast for our eyes to follow.
They only come out at night when it is dark.
p3-2-2.why: Bacteria are tiny living things. Only a microscope makes them big enough to see.

p3-2-2.text: Does a mushroom make its own food?
options: No. It soaks up food from around it.
Yes, it makes food in its cap, like a plant.
Only in the dark, under the soil.
Only when it rains for a whole day.
p3-2-2.why: A mushroom is a fungus, not a plant. Fungi cannot make their own food.

p3-2-2.text: Do all bacteria make us unwell?
options: No. Some bacteria help us, like in yoghurt.
Yes, all bacteria are harmful and make us ill.
No, only fungi can make us unwell.
Yes, every germ is bad for our bodies.
p3-2-2.why: Some bacteria help us. Some can make us unwell.

p3-2-2.text: Which of these is a fungus?
options: A bean plant in a pot.
p3-2-2.why: Yeast is a fungus. Mushrooms and bread mould are fungi too.

p3-2-2.text: Is the mould on old bread alive?
options: Yes. Mould is a living fungus.
No, it is just a dark stain on the bread.
No, it only grows on plastic and stones.
No, it is only dust that fell on it.
p3-2-2.why: Mould is a fungus. It is living: it grows and spreads over the bread.

p3-2-3.text: A creature spends all day in a pond. What can you say?
options: You need more clues before you decide.
It must be a fish, because it lives in water.
It must be an amphibian, because it swims.
p3-2-3.why: Many groups live in water. Check its covering and how its young are born before you decide.

p3-2-3.text: A creature with dry scales lays eggs on a warm bank. What is it?
options: A fish, because it swims well.
An amphibian, because it is near water.
A bird, because it lays eggs.
p3-2-3.why: Dry scales and eggs laid on land are reptile clues, even if it swims a lot.

p3-2-3.text: A creature with moist skin lays eggs in a pond. What is it?
options: A fish, because it lives in water.
A reptile, because it has four legs.
An insect, because it is small.
p3-2-3.why: Moist skin and eggs laid in water are amphibian clues.

p3-2-3.text: A creature with feathers cannot swim at all. What is it?
options: A bird. Feathers decide the group.
A mammal, because it cannot swim.
A reptile, because it walks on land.
A fish that lost its scales.
p3-2-3.why: Feathers mean bird, whether or not it swims or flies.

p3-2-3.text: What does "evidence" mean when you decide a group?
options: What you observe, like its covering and how its young are born.
A guess about how the animal looks.
p3-2-3.why: Evidence is what you observe. Good conclusions come from checking all of it.

p3-3-1.text: A backpack has a fabric body, a metal zip and a plastic tag. How many materials is it made of?
options: One, because it is one object
None, a backpack is not a material
p3-3-1.why: Fabric, metal and plastic are three different materials. One object can be made of many materials.

p3-3-1.text: Two cups look the same shape. Are they always made of the same material?
p3-3-1.why: The same kind of object can be made of different materials. One cup can be plastic, the other ceramic.

p3-3-1.text: Which of these names a material, not an object?
p3-3-1.why: Metal is a material. A spoon, a chair and a mug are objects that can be made of metal.

p3-3-1.text: A ruler can be made of wood or of plastic. What does this show?
options: The same kind of object can use different materials
p3-3-1.why: A ruler is one kind of object. It can be made of wood, plastic or even metal.

options: One material can make many different objects
A material can only make one object
Every object is made of exactly one material
Objects and materials are the same thing
p3-3-1.why: Wood can make a ruler, a chair and a door. One material can make many objects.

p3-3-2.text: A material that holds a heavy load without breaking is called
p3-3-2.why: Strong means it can hold a heavy load without breaking.

p3-3-2.text: The paper strip snapped after 2 weights. The plastic strip snapped after 6. Which is stronger?
p3-3-2.why: Plastic held more weights before it snapped, so plastic is stronger.

p3-3-2.text: A strip bends a lot before it breaks. Does that make it strong?
options: No. Strong means it holds a load.
Yes, bending a lot means it is strong.
Yes, bending is the same as strong.
p3-3-2.why: Bending is a different test. Strong is about holding a load without breaking.

p3-3-2.text: Which is a fair way to test strength?
options: Use strips of the same length and width
Add all the weights at once
p3-3-2.why: Only the material should be different. The strips must be the same size.

p3-3-2.text: Scissors are made of metal mainly because metal is
p3-3-2.why: Scissors must push hard without breaking. Metal is strong.

p3-3-3.text: A material that bends without breaking is called
p3-3-3.why: Flexible means it bends without breaking.

p3-3-3.text: The wood bent 2 cm. The plastic bent 6 cm under the same weight. Which is more flexible?
p3-3-3.why: Plastic bent further under the same weight, so plastic is more flexible.

p3-3-3.text: A glass sheet cracks after bending only a little. Is glass flexible?
options: No. It breaks before it bends much.
Yes. Any bending at all means it is flexible.
p3-3-3.why: Flexible means bending without breaking. Glass breaks, so it is not flexible.

p3-3-3.text: Which is a fair way to test how much strips bend?
options: Use strips of the same length and thickness
Use a different weight for each strip
p3-3-3.why: Only the material should change. Same length, same thickness, same weight.

p3-3-3.text: A rubber band bends a lot and does not snap. Rubber is
p3-3-3.why: Rubber bends a lot without breaking, so it is flexible.

p3-3-5.text: Which sheet did not let water through in our test?
p3-3-5.why: The drops sat on top of the plastic as beads. Underneath stayed dry.

p3-3-5.text: On the paper sheet, the water drops
options: sat on top as small round beads
p3-3-5.why: Paper soaks up water. The drops made a dark patch that grew.

p3-3-5.text: To keep the test fair, what should stay the same for both sheets?
options: The sheet size and number of drops
The colour and the shape of the sheet
The time of day and the weather
The name written on the sheet
p3-3-5.why: Only the material should change. Same size, same number of drops.

p3-3-5.text: A pupil wants to make a raincoat. Which material should be chosen?
options: Plastic, because it keeps water out
Fabric, because it is soft and soaks up water
Paper, because it is light and cheap to buy
Paper towel, because it is soft and thick
p3-3-5.why: A raincoat must keep water out. Plastic does not let water through.

p3-3-5.text: Which material soaks up water fastest?
p3-3-5.why: Paper towel soaks water up. Plastic, glass and metal do not let water through.

p3-3-6.text: Metal blocked every dot in our test. Metal lets
p3-3-6.why: No dots lit up behind the metal sheet. Metal lets no light through.

p3-3-6.text: Clear plastic lit up all five dots. Clear plastic lets
p3-3-6.why: All five dots lit up sharp and bright. Clear plastic lets most light through.

p3-3-6.text: Which sheet made a dark shadow on the screen?
p3-3-6.why: The metal sheet lets no light through, so it makes a dark shadow.

p3-3-6.text: Frosted plastic lit up 2 of the 5 dots, and they looked blurry. Frosted plastic lets
p3-3-6.why: A few blurry dots means some light gets through, but not most.

p3-3-6.text: Which is a fair way to test how much light passes through?
options: Use the same torch and distance each time
Use a brighter torch for one of the sheets
Test each sheet in a different dark room
Move the screen closer for each sheet
p3-3-6.why: Only the sheet should change. Same torch, same distance, same screen.

p3-3-7.text: A raincoat is made of plastic mainly because plastic
options: is strong enough to carry heavy bags
lets light through into the room
is shiny and pleasant to touch
p3-3-7.why: A raincoat must keep rain out. Plastic does not let water through.

p3-3-7.text: A window is made of glass mainly because glass
options: is flexible and bends in the wind
soaks up water from the rain
is heavy and hard to carry
p3-3-7.why: We look through windows. Glass lets light through.

p3-3-7.text: Which object needs a material that lets light through?
p3-3-7.why: We look through a window. Glass lets light through.

p3-3-7.text: A school bag strap is made of fabric mainly because fabric
options: soaks up water from the rain
p3-3-7.why: A strap must bend with you. Fabric is flexible.

p3-3-7.text: Scissors are made of metal mainly because metal
p3-3-7.why: Scissors push hard when they cut. Metal is strong and hard.

p3-3-8.text: Why do we improve an object?
options: To make it look different and colourful
To use up more of the materials
To make it heavier to carry around
p3-3-8.why: We change a material so the object does its job better.

p3-3-8.text: A paper strap tore easily. What is a good replacement?
options: Fabric, because it bends and is strong
Glass, because it is hard and see-through
Another paper strap, but a thicker one
Paper towel, because it is soft and thick
p3-3-8.why: A strap must bend and be strong. Fabric does both.

p3-3-8.text: Does any new material always make an object better?
options: No, it must suit the job
Yes, any change at all helps a lot
Only if it is made of metal or glass
Yes, if it is a new colour or shape
p3-3-8.why: Glass on a strap would break. The new material must suit the job.

p3-3-8.text: A leaking vase needs a material that
options: bends easily when it is held
p3-3-8.why: A vase holds water, so its material must not let water through.

p3-3-8.text: Which shows an improvement was really tested?
options: Comparing the weights before and after
Saying it looks much better than before
Asking a friend if it looks strong
p3-3-8.why: A test compares before and after. 2 weights before, 6 weights after.

p3-4-1.text: Which pair is a young living thing and the adult it grows into?
p3-4-1.why: A puppy grows into a dog, its own kind. A kitten grows into a cat.

p3-4-1.text: What happens to a young living thing over time?
options: It turns into a different kind
p3-4-1.why: Every living thing starts small and grows into an adult over time.

p3-4-1.text: A child and an adult person are alike because
options: both have the same body parts
both are the same height and weight
p3-4-1.why: The body parts are the same. The adult is bigger because it has grown more.
A seed grows into a plant of its own kind.

p3-4-1.text: The adult is different from the young because the adult
p3-4-1.why: The adult is the same kind, but it has grown bigger over time.

p3-4-2.text: What are the three stages of a plant's life cycle, in order?
p3-4-2.why: A seed grows into a seedling, and the seedling grows into an adult plant.

p3-4-2.text: What does a seed need to start growing?
options: Water, air and the right warmth
Only strong bright light from the sun
p3-4-2.why: Both seeds started growing, even the one in the dark. A seed needs water, air and warmth to start.

p3-4-2.text: The seedling in the dark box was pale and weak. Why?
options: A seedling needs light to grow well
It was given far too much water every day
p3-4-2.why: A seedling needs light to grow well. Without light it turns pale and weak.

p3-4-2.text: Where do a plant's new seeds come from?
options: Inside the fruit of the adult plant
From the roots under the ground
From the damp soil around its roots
p3-4-2.why: The adult plant grows flowers, then fruit. The new seeds are inside the fruit.

p3-4-2.text: On the windowsill, the sunny seedling grew from 1 cm to 12 cm. What does this show?
options: A seedling grows taller over the days
A seedling stays the same height each day
p3-4-2.why: A seedling grows taller each day when it has water, air and light.

p3-5-1.text: Which animal has three stages: egg, young and adult?
p3-5-1.why: A grasshopper has three stages. A butterfly, a mosquito and a beetle have four, with a pupa.

options: The animal turns back into an egg
p3-5-1.why: The pupa does not eat. Inside it, the adult is forming.

p3-5-1.text: A frog has three stages. Does the tadpole look like the adult frog?
options: No, it has a tail and lives in water
Yes, it looks exactly the same as the frog
Yes, but it is a lot smaller
p3-5-1.why: Three stages does not mean the young looks like the adult. A tadpole looks nothing like a frog.

p3-5-1.text: A caterpillar is the young of which animal?
p3-5-1.why: A caterpillar hatches from a butterfly egg, becomes a pupa, then an adult butterfly.

p3-5-1.text: The four stages of a mosquito, in order, are
p3-5-1.why: Egg, then larva in the water, then pupa, then the adult flies away.

p3-5-2.text: Two animals both start as an egg. Must they have the same number of stages?
options: No. A mosquito has four stages, a cockroach has three.
p3-5-2.why: Starting as an egg does not fix the number of stages. The mosquito has a pupa; the cockroach does not.

p3-5-2.text: A chicken and a frog both have three stages. Do their young look alike?
options: No. A chick looks like a hen, a tadpole looks nothing like a frog.
Yes. A chick and a tadpole both have feathers, so they look alike.
p3-5-2.why: The same number of stages does not mean the young look alike.

p3-5-2.text: Which of these has a pupa stage?
p3-5-2.why: Only four-stage animals like the mosquito and butterfly have a pupa.

p3-5-2.text: When we compare two life cycles, we look for
options: what is alike and what is different
only what is alike in the two life cycles
p3-5-2.why: Comparing means finding both the likenesses and the differences.

p3-5-2.text: The stages of a cockroach, in order, are
p3-5-2.why: A cockroach has three stages. The young looks like a small adult without wings.

p3-6-1a.text: A red end faces a blue end. What happens when the magnets slide close?
options: They repel and move apart from each other
p3-6-1a.why: Unlike poles, one red and one blue, attract.

p3-6-1a.text: Two red ends face each other. What happens?
options: They always stick, whatever ends face
p3-6-1a.why: Like poles, both red or both blue, repel.

p3-6-1a.text: A magnet is turned round so the other end faces. Does it stop being a magnet?
options: No. It still attracts or repels, depending on the ends.
Yes. Turning it round makes it stop working for good.
Yes, until it is turned back.
p3-6-1a.why: Turning a magnet only changes which end faces. Both ends are still poles.

p3-6-1a.text: Can U-shaped magnets repel each other?
p3-6-1a.why: The rule is the same for every shape: like poles repel.

p3-6-1a.text: Which pair of poles will attract?
p3-6-1a.why: Unlike poles attract. Like poles repel.

p3-6-1b.text: Does a magnet attract anything made of metal?
options: No. It attracts only some metals, like iron and steel.
Yes, if the metal is shiny.
Yes, if the metal is heavy.
p3-6-1b.why: The copper coin and the foil are metal, but the magnet did not attract them.

p3-6-1b.text: Why was the shiny foil not attracted?
options: It is not made of a magnetic material
It was too thin for the magnet to hold
It was too shiny for the magnet to grip
p3-6-1b.why: Shiny does not mean magnetic. Foil is not iron or steel.

p3-6-1b.text: Can a plastic ruler become magnetic if it is painted grey?
options: No. Paint does not change what it is made of.
Yes, grey paint turns it into a magnetic material.
Only if the paint is thick.
p3-6-1b.why: A magnet attracts because of the material, not the colour.
Iron is a magnetic material. The nail jumped to the magnet.

p3-6-1b.text: A steel paper clip shivers and then jumps to the magnet. This shows that steel is
p3-6-1b.why: Steel is attracted by a magnet, so steel is a magnetic material.

p3-6-2.text: Where does a magnet attract most strongly?
options: At its two ends, the poles
Only at the red end, not the blue end
p3-6-2.why: Both ends held 8 clips. The middle held only 1.

p3-6-2.text: Does a U-shaped magnet have poles?
options: No, only bar magnets have poles
p3-6-2.why: Every magnet has two poles, whatever its shape.

p3-6-2.text: Why do we count the clips?
options: More clips means a stronger attraction at that spot
The number of clips does not tell us anything at all
p3-6-2.why: The number of clips tells us how strongly that spot attracts.

p3-6-2.text: Which spot of the bar magnet held the fewest clips?
p3-6-2.why: The middle held only 1 clip. Each end held 8.

p3-6-2.text: The middle of the bar magnet held 1 clip. The ends held 8. This shows
options: the ends attract more strongly than the middle
the magnet is broken because the middle held so few
p3-6-2.why: More clips at the ends means stronger attraction at the poles.

p3-6-3a.text: Red faces blue. What do the carts do?
p3-6-3a.why: Unlike poles attract, so the carts roll together.

p3-6-3a.text: Red faces red. What do the carts do?
p3-6-3a.why: Like poles repel, so the carts stay apart.

p3-6-3a.text: Do the carts need a hand to move them apart when like poles face?
options: No. The magnets repel without touching.
Yes, unless the track is very long and flat.
p3-6-3a.why: Magnets attract and repel without touching. No hand is needed.
Repel means they move apart. Attract means they come together.

p3-6-3a.text: Do two magnets always roll together, whatever ends face?
options: No. It depends which ends face.
Yes, if they are both on little carts.
p3-6-3a.why: Unlike poles attract and like poles repel. It depends which ends face.

p3-6-3b.text: Two ring magnets float apart with a gap. The sides facing each other are
p3-6-3b.why: A gap means like poles are facing. Like poles repel.

p3-6-3b.text: A ring sits flat on another ring. The sides facing each other are
p3-6-3b.why: Flat means unlike poles are facing. Unlike poles attract.

p3-6-3b.text: A ring floats above another ring. Is the magnet broken?
options: No. Like poles are repelling, which is normal.
Yes, rings should always sit flat on each other.
Only if the gap is big.
p3-6-3b.why: Floating is what like poles do. The magnets are working.

p3-6-3b.text: Will any two ring magnets always float apart?
options: No. It depends which sides face.
Yes, if they are exactly the same size.
p3-6-3b.why: Turn one ring over and they sit flat. It depends which sides face.

p3-6-3b.text: A ring floats above a blue side. Its hidden side must be
p3-6-3b.why: A gap means the same colour is facing. Blue below, blue hidden.

p3-6-3c.text: An object is attracted by one pole and repelled by the other. It is
p3-6-3c.why: Only a magnet can be repelled, because it has poles of its own.

p3-6-3c.text: An object is attracted by both poles. It is
p3-6-3c.why: A magnetic material like iron is attracted by either pole and never repelled.

p3-6-3c.text: Must any object attracted to a magnet be a magnet itself?
options: No. An iron nail is attracted but is not a magnet.
Yes, if it is shiny and made of metal, it must be a magnet.
p3-6-3c.why: A magnetic material is attracted too. To be sure, test the other pole: a magnet is repelled.

p3-6-3c.text: An object is repelled by one pole. Could it be non-magnetic?
options: No. Only a magnet can be repelled.
p3-6-3c.why: A non-magnetic material does nothing near a magnet. Repelling means it is a magnet.

p3-6-3c.text: Why do we test with both poles?
options: To tell a magnet from a magnetic material
To make the magnet warm enough to work well
Because red is easier to see
p3-6-3c.why: Both attract a magnetic material. Only a magnet is repelled by one of them.

p3-6-4.text: A hanging magnet is nudged and settles again. Which way does it point?
p3-6-4.why: A magnet free to turn always settles the same way: north–south.

p3-6-4.text: Does only a bar magnet settle pointing one way?
options: No. Any magnet free to turn does.
Yes, only long bar magnets settle like this.
p3-6-4.why: Hanging, floating or in a compass: any free magnet settles north–south.

options: a small magnet free to turn
a magnet that is stuck and never moves
p3-6-4.why: The needle is a tiny magnet. That is why it settles north–south.

p3-6-4.text: Does a compass needle point wherever it is pushed?
options: No. It swings back and settles north–south.
Yes, it stays pointing wherever you push it.
p3-6-4.why: Push it and it swings back. A free magnet always settles the same way.

p3-6-4.text: A magnet floats on a board in water. When it stops turning, it points
options: towards the nearest side of the basin
p3-6-4.why: Floating lets the magnet turn freely, so it settles north–south.

p3-7-1a.text: Why does an iron nail become a magnet when stroked, but a copper rod does not?
options: Iron is a magnetic material and copper is not
Copper is too shiny and too soft to become a magnet
The copper rod was stroked too fast
p3-7-1a.why: Only a magnetic material like iron or steel can be made into a magnet.

p3-7-1a.text: How should we stroke the nail to make it a magnet?
options: With one pole, the same way each time, lifting away after each stroke
Any way at all, direction does not matter
Rubbing it back and forth quickly, keeping the magnet on the nail all the time
p3-7-1a.why: One pole, one direction, lift away each time. Back and forth undoes the work.

p3-7-1a.text: A nail is stroked 40 times instead of 10. What happens to the number of clips it attracts?
p3-7-1a.why: More strokes make a stronger magnet, up to a point.

p3-7-1a.text: Which of these will become a magnet when stroked with a bar magnet?
p3-7-1a.why: Steel is a magnetic material. Plastic, wood and copper are not.

p3-7-1a.text: The nail held 2 clips after 10 strokes and 7 after 40. What does this show?
options: More strokes make a stronger magnet
Fewer strokes make a stronger magnet
The nail was a magnet from the start
p3-7-1a.why: More strokes gave more clips, so the magnet was stronger.

p3-7-1b.text: When is the nail a magnet in this experiment?
options: Only while electricity flows through the wire
All the time, even before the battery is connected
Only after it is stroked with a bar magnet
p3-7-1b.why: Connect the battery and the clips cling. Disconnect it and they drop.

p3-7-1b.text: What happens when the battery is disconnected?
options: The nail stops being a magnet and the clips drop away
The nail stays a magnet forever
The nail becomes a stronger magnet and holds more clips
p3-7-1b.why: No electricity, no magnet. The clips drop away.

p3-7-1b.text: A nail is wound with 30 turns of wire instead of 10, using the same battery. What happens to the number of clips it attracts?
p3-7-1b.why: More turns of wire make a stronger magnet made with electricity.

p3-7-1b.text: Why is a magnet made with electricity useful in a crane that lifts scrap metal?
options: It can be switched off to drop the metal where wanted
It never needs a battery or any wire to work well
It is lighter than a bar magnet
p3-7-1b.why: Switch it on to lift, off to drop. A bar magnet cannot be switched off.

p3-7-1b.text: What do we coil the wire around to make this kind of magnet?
p3-7-1b.why: Iron is a magnetic material. Wood, plastic and copper are not.

p3-7-2.text: Why do we choose a magnet's pole on purpose when building a toy?
options: To make the toy attract or repel as we planned
To make the magnet look nicer
So that the toy can use more magnets than before
Because red is the strong end
p3-7-2.why: Which poles face decides attract or repel. We choose it to fit the plan.

p3-7-2.text: Two magnets move apart when they face each other. What poles are facing?
options: Like poles, such as red facing red
Unlike poles, such as red facing blue
p3-7-2.why: Like poles repel. Unlike poles attract.

p3-7-2.text: A toy cart will not move toward the wand. What could improve it?
options: Flip a magnet's pole, or move the wand closer
Paint the cart a new colour
Swap the magnet for a plastic part
Add a much heavier flag at the end of the track
p3-7-2.why: Wrong poles, or too far away. Change one of those and test again.

p3-7-2.text: Why do we test a toy after building it?
options: To find out if it really works the way we planned
Testing is only needed if the toy looks wrong at first
p3-7-2.why: A test shows what really happens. Then we can improve it.

p3-7-2.text: Which of these shows a toy was really improved?
options: Comparing how it worked before and after one change
Saying that it looks a lot better now than it did before
p3-7-2.why: 10 cm, then 25, then 40: the attempts show the change helped.

spotsort.text: A puddle moves when it is windy. Is the puddle living?
options: No. The wind pushes it. It does not grow or need food.
Yes. A puddle moves along the ground, so it must be living.
Yes. A puddle is wet, so it must be living.
Yes. A puddle is outside, so it must be living.
spotsort.why: Moving is not enough. A living thing moves by itself, grows and needs air, water and food. A puddle does none of these.

spotsort.text: A seed sits still on the shelf. Is it living?
options: Yes. It can grow into a plant.
No. It does not move, so it is non-living.
No. It is small, so it is non-living.
No. It is brown, so it is non-living.
spotsort.why: A seed looks still, but it can grow into a plant. Growing is a clue for a living thing.

spotsort.text: A bicycle moves when someone pedals it. Is it living?
options: No. It cannot move by itself. It does not grow.
Yes. It moves, so it is living.
Yes. It has a bell and two wheels, so it is living.
No. It is made of metal, and metal things cannot move.
spotsort.why: The bicycle only moves because someone pedals it. It does not grow and does not need air, water or food.

spotsort.text: A cat is fast asleep and not moving. Is it still living?
options: Yes. It still needs air, water and food.
No. It is not moving, so it is not living now.
Yes. It is soft, so it is living.
Yes. It has fur, so it is living.
spotsort.why: A sleeping cat is still living. It still breathes, needs water and food, and can grow.

spotsort.text: What do all living things need?
spotsort.why: Every living thing needs air, water and food. Living things can also grow, respond and make new living things like themselves.
